paragraphs.text: Solar panels need space, and in crowded countries land is expensive. One solution is to place panels on water. Floating solar farms have been built on reservoirs, lakes and even flooded quarries.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Water has an unexpected advantage: it keeps the panels cool. Solar panels work less efficiently when they are hot, and tests in Singapore found that floating panels produced up to 10 per cent more electricity than similar panels on nearby rooftops.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The panels also shade the water, which reduces evaporation. This is particularly useful for reservoirs that supply drinking water in dry regions.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Engineers are still studying the effects on wildlife. Covering too much of a lake could reduce the light reaching underwater plants, so most projects cover no more than a third of the surface.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Several countries in Asia and Europe are now planning much larger floating farms, some covering areas the size of hundreds of football pitches.
paragraphs.label: E

items.prompt: Apart from reservoirs and lakes, where have floating solar farms been built?
In which country were the floating panels tested?
By how much more electricity did the floating panels produce?
What does the shade from the panels reduce?
What is the largest part of a lake’s surface that most projects cover?
